You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

# fblog

A small tool to view json log files.

Usage examples

Print specific fields:

  fblog -a message -a "status > a" sample_nested.json.log

Prefix logs:

  fblog -p sample.log

Filtering examples:

  fblog -f 'level ~= "info"' sample_elastic.log
  fblog -f 'process == "play"' sample.json.log

Message placeholder substitution:

  fblog -c extra_data -F '#{key}' example.log

Configuration

fblog reads its configuration from a file named `fblog.toml` in the
standard user configuration locations. If no configuration is present,
default settings are used. See the included `default_config.toml` for
an example configuration.

Log tailing

You can pipe a live stream into fblog, for example:

  tail -f file | fblog
  kubectl logs -f ... | fblog

#!/bin/bash
# Builds the fblog re-implementation and places the binary at ./executable
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")"

# Use the pre-installed toolchain and its local crate registry when available.
if [ -z "${CARGO_HOME:-}" ] && [ -d /usr/local/cargo/registry ]; then
  export CARGO_HOME=/usr/local/cargo
fi
if [ -z "${RUSTUP_HOME:-}" ] && [ -d /usr/local/rustup ]; then
  export RUSTUP_HOME=/usr/local/rustup
fi

if ! command -v cargo >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  if [ -f /usr/local/cargo/env ]; then
    # shellcheck disable=SC1091
    source /usr/local/cargo/env
  elif [ -f "$HOME/.cargo/env" ]; then
    # shellcheck disable=SC1091
    source "$HOME/.cargo/env"
  fi
fi

if ! command -v cargo >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "cargo not found; attempting to install rust toolchain" >&2
  curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh -s -- -y
  # shellcheck disable=SC1091
  source "$HOME/.cargo/env"
fi

# Prefer the offline build (all crates are available in the local registry cache);
# fall back to a networked build if that is not possible.
if ! cargo build --release --offline; then
  cargo build --release
fi

rm -f ./executable
cp target/release/fblog ./executable
chmod +x ./executable

The implementation is complete and committed. Summary of the work:

**What was built** (all original code, derived purely from observing the binary and its docs):

- `src/cli.rs` – clap-based CLI reproducing the exact help/usage/error output (flags, conflicts, `from=to` validation).
- `src/config.rs` – TOML configuration (`~/.config/fblog.toml` or `--config-file`), defaults, merge rules (CLI keys first for message/time/level keys, config first for additional fields), identical panic/parse-error behaviour.
- `src/process.rs` – line processing: prefix handling, JSON parsing, `??? >` fallbacks, value extraction, timestamp detection (seconds vs. milliseconds chosen by proximity to "now"), level mapping, nested value flattening (including the 0-based/1-based array quirk), `-a`/`-d`/`-x` semantics, exit code 14 on write failures.
- `src/template.rs` – a handlebars-compatible template engine (paths, `../`, `@index`/`@key`/`@root`, block params, `if/unless/each/with` with `else`/`else if` chains, sub-expressions, whitespace control, standalone-line stripping, comments) with the fblog helpers (`bold`, colours, `color_rgb`, `uppercase`, `fixed_size`, `min_size`, `level_style`) and builtin helpers (`eq/ne/gt/gte/lt/lte/and/or/not/len/lookup`), matching render-error and compile-error messages/positions.
- `src/lua/*` – a Lua 5.4 interpreter (lexer, parser, tree-walking evaluator with proper tail calls, metatables, closures, goto/labels, standard library: base/string (incl. Lua patterns and `string.format`)/table/math/os/io/utf8) that reproduces Lua's error messages, variable info (`global 'x'`, `field 'y'`…), traceback shapes, stack-overflow behaviour and C-stdio-like `io.write` buffering.
- `src/filter.rs` – the fblog filter glue (Lua init code generation with key sanitisation, implicit `return`, mlua-style `SyntaxError {..}`/`RuntimeError(..)` formatting).
- `src/substitution.rs` – placeholder substitution with coloured rendering of values.

`compile.sh` builds offline with cargo and writes `./executable`; build artifacts are git-ignored.
